packs.title: Columns, Collections and Water
packs.promise: Find copper dragons, a suspended sphere and a half-moon pond, then make the city your own observation notebook.

q.s: Make a small composition from a very large square.
st: From a stopped public spot, find the blue-and-white hall, a roofline at the side of the square and a patch of open paving. Leave any ceremony or rehearsal area clear.
Draw three tiny frames, or write three short scene descriptions. In the first, make the hall the focus; in the second, let a side roof lead the eye; in the third, make the open space the subject.
Give your sequence a short title. Save it with one sentence about which framing changed your impression most.

q.s: Match an animal's needs to the space around it.
st: Use today's map and open paths to choose two nearby animal exhibits. Read their habitat or behaviour information; the Taiwan native-animal area is one possible starting area, subject to current closures.

Collect one need for each animal from its label, then find a visible design feature that could meet it: a perch, shade, water, cover or a digging space. Separate what the label says from your own design interpretation.
Save the two need-and-feature pairs. Add one question you would ask a habitat designer. An animal hiding or resting does not prevent this task.

q.s: Turn an object in the collection into a new drawing.
st: Choose an object currently displayed in an open gallery and read its label. Record its name and one visible maker's choice: a handle, edge, pattern, joint or silhouette. No particular famous object must be on display.
Make an original drawing of a useful everyday object that borrows just that one choice. Alternatively, write a small design brief explaining the borrowed feature and the new object's purpose.
Save the design with a credit line naming the museum object that inspired it. Separate the label's facts from your own invention.

packs.title: Dadaocheng in Two Afternoons
packs.promise: Follow letters, fabric and tea work from Beimen's museums to the Tamsui River.

q.t: Follow One Thing through the City
q.s: Gather the links between cargo and a changing Taipei.
st: In the permanent displays about Taipei's industry, transport and urban change, choose one named good, trade or transport system that catches your attention.

Collect two connected pieces of evidence from the displays: one about how it moved or was handled, and one about a place, worker or city change connected to it. Use the labels to check the relationship rather than inventing a history.
Save a small chain diagram or a few sentences linking the evidence. Mark any unanswered link as a question.

q.s: Find how fabric patterns suit different imagined uses.
st: Look at fabrics visibly offered from the customer aisles and find two contrasting pattern scales: one that reads from a distance and one whose detail appears close up.

Collect each as a written description or small drawing. Give it an imagined use, such as a curtain, a sleeve or a bag, and explain how the scale would work there. Treat the use as your design idea, not a claim about the seller's product.
Save the two pattern-and-purpose entries. Compare what would change if you swapped their uses.

q.s: Turn a tea factory's rooms into a small visual story.
st: Find the first-floor interpretation of hand sorting, air separation and roasting. Check the labels or the museum's easy-read guide for what happened in each room; do not assume a machine is operating.
Create three small original scenes showing tea passing through those stages. Use drawings, a short comic or three written scene directions. Give each stage an action based on the interpretation.
Save the sequence with one sentence about how the work changes from hands to machinery and heat. Keep any imagined dialogue separate from factual explanation.
